# Integrating a Pan-African Banking Group
## Nigeria · Kenya · Morocco — three licenses, three supervisors, one product ambition

---

## 1. The core diagnosis

The board bought "a pan-African bank." What was legally acquired is **three separately capitalised, separately supervised, separately resolvable banks that happen to share a shareholder.** Almost every integration failure in this deal class comes from managing the first sentence while being governed by the second.

Four reframes before any plan:

**1. The binding constraint is not technology. It is capital and liquidity non-fungibility.**
Naira, shilling and dirham liquidity are not one pool. Nigerian FX repatriation is administered, not automatic. Each supervisor requires its entity to survive the failure of the group. So the classic acquirer move — centralise treasury, run one balance sheet, extract funding synergies — is largely unavailable. Synergy must come from somewhere else (§5).

**2. "One core banking system" is the wrong promise.** It is the promise most likely to be made in month two and abandoned in month thirty, having consumed the integration budget and the credibility of the CIO. Commit instead to **one customer experience, one data spine, one control framework — three ledgers for now.**

**3. Regulators are not a compliance workstream. They are a stakeholder group with veto power over your sequencing.** CBN, CBK and Bank Al-Maghrib will each independently approve outsourcing, cloud hosting, core migration, brand change, board appointments and dividend upstreaming. A migration plan that is technically elegant and un-approvable is worth nothing.

**4. The scarce asset is deposit trust, and it is local.** In all three markets the deposit franchise is attached to a local name, local branch managers, and in Nigeria and Kenya to specific relationship bankers who can walk deposits out of the door. Brand and people decisions are therefore *liquidity* decisions, not marketing and HR decisions.

**Governing pattern: group architecture, local execution, deliberate divergence where the law or the language requires it.** Standardise the ledger of record for risk, capital, data models and controls. Localise the ledger of record for customers, rails, identity and brand.

---

## 2. Five non-negotiables (set before any migration begins)

### 2.1 The severability test
No integration step may create a dependency that would prevent any one entity from operating standalone for 90 days. Every shared service is documented with an exit plan and a local fallback. This is what makes cloud, shared processing hubs and group platforms approvable — and it is also simply true risk management in markets with FX and sovereign volatility.

### 2.2 Two-key decision rights
Any change touching **a customer, a ledger, or a regulator** requires two signatures: the group owner of the standard, and the local entity CEO. Neither can act alone. Reserved matters (risk appetite, capital actions, model approval, brand, core selection) sit with group; everything else defaults local. Published as a two-page RACI on day 1, because ambiguity here is what produces the "second CEO" problem.

### 2.3 Control functions report up; revenue functions report local
CRO, CFO, Head of Financial Crime, CISO and CIO in each entity have a **hard line to group** and a dotted line to the local CEO (subject to local fit-and-proper and board approval). Distribution, SME, retail and corporate coverage report **local**, full stop. Parachuting group expatriates into revenue roles destroys the deposit franchise; not owning the control functions destroys the group.

### 2.4 Data residency by design
Assume in-country primary storage and processing for customer and payments data (Nigeria NDPA; Kenya's DPA and localisation expectations for certain data; Morocco's CNDP regime and its distinct French/EU-facing posture). The group data platform is **federated**: an in-country node holds records, and only defined aggregates, risk metrics and de-identified analytics cross borders, under documented lawful bases. Design this in month one; retrofitting it costs a year.

### 2.5 Financial crime is a revenue programme, not a cost centre
Correspondent banking access and cross-border corridor products live or die on AML/CFT credibility. One group financial-crime standard, calibrated to the strictest of the three supervisors, is the precondition for the entire cross-border revenue thesis. De-risking by a USD correspondent is the single fastest way to destroy this deal.

---

## 3. Technology: hollow out, don't rip out

The architecture is a layer cake. Standardise downward from the customer; leave the ledger for last.

| Layer | Strategy | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| **Channels / experience** (app, web, USSD, agent, branch teller UI) | **One group platform**, three localisations | Where customers perceive "one bank." Highest visible value, lowest regulatory friction |
| **Product & orchestration** (onboarding, lending workflow, pricing, limits) | **One group layer**, country product catalogues | Where speed-to-market synergy actually lives |
| **Data & analytics** | **One model, federated nodes** | Credit scoring, collections, pricing uplift — the biggest hard-number synergy |
| **Financial crime, risk, finance** | **One group engine, local instances** | Regulatory leverage + correspondent credibility |
| **Core ledger** | **Keep local; rationalise on a business case, per entity** | Highest cost, highest risk, lowest customer-visible value |
| **Payments rails, switch, identity/KYC** | **Local, permanently** | NIBSS/NIP, PesaLink/M-Pesa integration, Morocco's rails and national ID regimes are non-negotiable local infrastructure |

**Migration pattern: progressive strangulation.** Wrap each existing core in an API façade against a canonical group data model. All *new* products launch on the group stack from month ~12. The legacy book converts only when (a) the vendor contract or the platform's risk profile forces it, (b) the entity's cost-to-income case clears a defined hurdle, or (c) a single scheduled conversion event is safer than dual-running. Big-bang core replacement across three countries in parallel is not a strategy; it is a chapter in someone's post-mortem.

**Expect a two-core, not one-core, end state.** Morocco's language environment (French/Arabic), participative-banking product set, and European-facing regulatory orientation make a shared core with Lagos and Nairobi a poor fit. Plan for a West/East Africa target core and a Morocco core, joined by the data and experience layers. Declaring this early is cheaper than discovering it in year three.

---

## 4. Sequencing

### Phase 0 — Pre-close and Day 1 (months −6 to 0): **Continuity**
Approvals, fit-and-proper filings, local board reconstitution, retention agreements for the top ~150 (revenue owners and named regulatory role-holders first), Day-1 continuity plan, no customer-visible change, endorsement branding only. Day 1 communication in the local language, delivered by the local CEO, not by group.
*Deliverable: nothing breaks; nobody senior leaves; no regulator is surprised.*

### Phase 1 — Months 0–9: **Control and confidence**
- Consolidated risk appetite; harmonised IFRS 9 staging, ECL models, provisioning policy; **chart-of-accounts mapping** (not migration) for a single group MI pack within 120 days.
- Group treasury *visibility* (not centralisation): daily liquidity, FX exposure, sovereign concentration.
- AML/KYC uplift to group standard; cyber and access-control baseline; close the audit findings the sellers left behind.
- Regulator engagement rhythm established (§6).
- **Zero customer-visible change. Zero brand change. Zero core touching.**

### Phase 2 — Months 9–24: **One bank to the customer**
- Group experience layer live in one market first (Kenya — best digital maturity, most benign supervisory posture for innovation), then Nigeria (scale), then Morocco (localisation-heaviest).
- First corridor products: diaspora remittance, intra-Africa trade finance, multi-currency accounts for corporates operating in ≥2 of the three markets, card issuance/acceptance on a group scheme relationship.
- Federated data platform; first group credit-scoring and collections models deployed locally.
- Procurement consolidation and vendor renegotiation (the least glamorous, fastest-paying synergy).
- Endorsed branding rolls out: *"[Local Bank], part of [Group]."*

### Phase 3 — Months 24–42: **Rationalisation**
- Core migration in the entity with the weakest platform, one country at a time, never two conversions in one quarter, never in the same quarter as a brand change.
- Shared services hubs: Nairobi (technology, data, engineering), Casablanca (francophone operations, treasury support, French/Arabic servicing). Sequenced so no entity fails the severability test.
- Branch and channel network optimisation — *after* the digital alternative exists, not before.
- Morocco labour and social-dialogue processes handled on a longer clock than Nigeria and Kenya; assume 12–18 months for any restructuring with headcount impact.

### Phase 4 — Months 42–60: **Consolidation and platform monetisation**
- Brand endpoint decision executed (§7).
- Next acquisitions run through a now-tested integration factory — the Nigerian recapitalisation cycle and Kenyan capital step-ups are producing sellers; the group's advantage is that it can integrate, not that it can buy.
- Consider licensing the platform, or extending Morocco as the francophone West Africa beachhead.

---

## 5. Where the money actually comes from

Because funding synergies are constrained, the value case must be explicit and evidence-gated. Rough ordering by reliability:

| Source | Reliability | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Procurement, vendor and licence consolidation | High | Fast, unsexy, real |
| Risk-model and collections uplift (best-of-three deployed everywhere) | High | Often the largest single item; needs the data layer |
| RWA and capital optimisation *within each entity* | Medium-high | Not across; each supervisor ring-fences |
| Technology run-cost convergence | Medium | Only materialises after core rationalisation; back-load it |
| Cross-border corridor revenue (trade, remittance, corporate FX) | Medium | Contingent on financial-crime credibility |
| Product velocity (one build, three launches) | Medium | Contingent on the orchestration layer |
| Branch/headcount reduction | Low early | Deposit and political risk; Morocco labour constraints |
| Funding-cost synergies | Low | Structurally limited |

Two reporting disciplines: **(a)** report synergies in constant currency *and* reported currency — a naira devaluation can erase a genuinely successful integration in the group P&L, and the board must be able to tell the difference; **(b)** no synergy counts until the local CFO signs it, to kill double-counting between group and entity plans.

---

## 6. Regulatory strategy

**One narrative, three calendars.** The same integration story, in the same sequence, told to CBN, CBK and BAM — with dates and dependencies specific to each. Iron rule: **no supervisor learns anything material about the group from another supervisor first.**

- **Front the local CEO.** Group CRO attends; group CEO appears at milestones. A supervisor whose primary relationship is with a foreign executive treats the entity as a branch of a foreign risk.
- **Push for a supervisory college / MOU set** early, anchored on wherever the holdco is domiciled. Consolidated supervision is coming whether or not you invite it; inviting it buys goodwill and predictability.
- **Pre-clear the pattern, not just the transaction:** cloud hosting, outsourcing to group hubs, intragroup service agreements at arm's-length pricing, core migration protocol, brand change notification. Get an approved template once per country rather than a fresh negotiation per project.
- **Local commitment ledger:** track every undertaking given to each regulator (lending to priority sectors, local employment, branch presence, data hosting, capital retention) as hard constraints in the integration plan. Breaching a Phase-0 commitment in Phase 3 because nobody wrote it down is a standard, avoidable disaster.
- Capital: treat Nigerian and Kenyan minimum-capital step-ups as fixed dates on the master plan, funded from the group with pre-agreed injection mechanics — not as a surprise in year two.

---

## 7. Brand: endorse, then decide with evidence

Three options, and the honest answer is that it varies by market.

| Option | When it fits | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| **Retain local brands indefinitely, group as endorser** | Strong incumbent trust, politically sensitive market, deposit-heavy retail | Weak group equity, duplicated marketing, no corridor pull |
| **Endorsed transition → single group masterbrand** | Where group brand adds credibility (cards, corridors, corporate, diaspora) | Deposit attrition if mistimed |
| **Dual architecture: group brand for products, local brand for the bank** | Most likely answer here | Requires disciplined brand governance |

**Sequencing rules:**
1. Endorsement from Day 1 — universal, cheap, reversible.
2. Group masterbrand on **corridor and digital products first** (multi-currency, remittance, cards, trade), where the group name is an asset and there is no legacy trust to lose.
3. Full masterbrand conversion of a bank **only after** 4+ consecutive quarters of stable-or-growing deposits, a completed core-conversion elsewhere in the calendar, and a local market test.
4. Never in the same quarter as: a core migration, a branch closure programme, a national election, or a currency event.
5. Likeliest end state: single masterbrand in Nigeria and Kenya (Anglophone, digital-forward, group name travels), longer endorsement or permanent dual identity in Morocco, where the local name carries francophone and participative-banking credibility that a Lagos- or Nairobi-facing brand cannot.

---

## 8. Management alignment

**Structure.** A small Group Integration Office (~15 FTE, reporting to the Group CEO, chaired by a COO-calibre leader with authority, not a PMO administrator), plus a full-time local integration lead in each country with a hard line to the GIO and a seat on the local ExCo. Local integration leads should be respected internal appointees, not group imports.

**The "second CEO" problem.** Acquired-bank MDs in these markets are often locally powerful, board-endorsed, and personally attached to the deposit book. Do not fight them and do not neuter them. Give them: the local P&L, the regulator relationship, distribution, and a genuine seat in group product prioritisation. Take from them: risk, finance, financial crime, technology architecture, and pricing standards. Write it down in the reserved-matters list in month one. Retention windows of 24–36 months with cliffs aligned
